academic_reading.prompt: What is one purpose of repair events?
academic_reading.explanation: They can transfer practical knowledge.
academic_reading.passage_text:
For decades, many household products were designed around replacement rather than repair. Recently, however, repair has become more visible through tool libraries, repair cafés and online instruction. These activities can extend the useful life of everyday objects while also transferring practical knowledge between generations.

Businesses are responding unevenly. Some manufacturers publish repair manuals or sell components directly, but a manual is of little use if a replacement part is unavailable. Researchers therefore distinguish between willingness and opportunity: people may want to repair an item but lack time, tools, information or confidence.

There is also an environmental argument. Extending a product's life can delay the costs associated with producing and transporting a replacement. The size of that benefit varies by product, so repair is best viewed as one part of a wider strategy for reducing material waste.

academic_reading.prompt: Why are urban trees treated as infrastructure?
academic_reading.explanation: The passage identifies shade, air movement and rainwater benefits.
academic_reading.passage_text:
Urban trees are increasingly treated as infrastructure rather than decoration. Their canopies can reduce direct sunlight, influence local air movement and help manage rainwater. These benefits matter particularly in dense neighbourhoods dominated by hard surfaces.

Species differ in canopy size, growth rate, water needs and pollution tolerance. A fast-growing tree may provide shade quickly but require more maintenance later. Planning must also consider underground pipes, cables and foundations because roots need adequate growing space.

Residents can influence whether tree programmes succeed. During establishment, trees need care and protection. Where residents understand why species and locations were selected, support can be stronger. Effective programmes therefore combine ecological knowledge, engineering constraints and social planning.

academic_reading.prompt: What is a transactive memory system in practice?
options: A group knows where knowledge is located
academic_reading.explanation: Members learn who is likely to know what.
academic_reading.passage_text:
Teams can develop shared ways of remembering. One person may remember a customer preference while another recalls technical history; together they can reconstruct information that neither could easily retrieve alone. This works best when members understand who is likely to know what.

Technology can strengthen or weaken this process. Searchable records reduce dependence on personal memory, but excessive documentation can cause people to stop learning information they may need. Teams are also vulnerable to shared errors: repeated incorrect explanations can increase confidence without improving accuracy.

The strongest systems combine human knowledge with external records. People provide context, judgement and flexible interpretation, while records provide stable reference points. Important assumptions still need checking, especially when decisions have significant consequences.

academic_reading.prompt: Which passage discusses material waste?

academic_reading.passage_text:
For decades, many household products were designed around replacement rather than repair. Recently, however, repair has become more visible through tool libraries, repair cafés and online instruction. These activities can extend the useful life of everyday objects while also transferring practical knowledge between generations.

Businesses are responding unevenly. Some manufacturers publish repair manuals or sell components directly, but a manual is of little use if a replacement part is unavailable. Researchers therefore distinguish between willingness and opportunity: people may want to repair an item but lack time, tools, information or confidence.

There is also an environmental argument. Extending a product's life can delay the costs associated with producing and transporting a replacement. The size of that benefit varies by product, so repair is best viewed as one part of a wider strategy for reducing material waste.

Species differ in canopy size, growth rate, water needs and pollution tolerance. A fast-growing tree may provide shade quickly but require more maintenance later. Planning must also consider underground pipes, cables and foundations because roots need adequate growing space.

Residents can influence whether tree programmes succeed. During establishment, trees need care and protection. Where residents understand why species and locations were selected, support can be stronger. Effective programmes therefore combine ecological knowledge, engineering constraints and social planning.

general_reading.prompt: What might one team member remember?
general_reading.explanation: A customer preference is the opening example.
general_reading.passage_text:
Teams can develop shared ways of remembering. One person may remember a customer preference while another recalls technical history; together they can reconstruct information that neither could easily retrieve alone. This works best when members understand who is likely to know what.

Technology can strengthen or weaken this process. Searchable records reduce dependence on personal memory, but excessive documentation can cause people to stop learning information they may need. Teams are also vulnerable to shared errors: repeated incorrect explanations can increase confidence without improving accuracy.

The strongest systems combine human knowledge with external records. People provide context, judgement and flexible interpretation, while records provide stable reference points. Important assumptions still need checking, especially when decisions have significant consequences.

general_reading.prompt: Which passage discusses material waste?
general_reading.explanation: R1 discusses reducing material waste.
general_reading.passage_text:
For decades, many household products were designed around replacement rather than repair. Recently, however, repair has become more visible through tool libraries, repair cafés and online instruction. These activities can extend the useful life of everyday objects while also transferring practical knowledge between generations.

Businesses are responding unevenly. Some manufacturers publish repair manuals or sell components directly, but a manual is of little use if a replacement part is unavailable. Researchers therefore distinguish between willingness and opportunity: people may want to repair an item but lack time, tools, information or confidence.

There is also an environmental argument. Extending a product's life can delay the costs associated with producing and transporting a replacement. The size of that benefit varies by product, so repair is best viewed as one part of a wider strategy for reducing material waste.
